issues.title: Make outer certificate binding critical
issues.author: davidben
issues.body: @aarongable pointed out that, due to how ACME DV challenges work (sadness), we may need to make the semantics of the certificate somewhat dependent on the particular outer CA that the alternate CA is channeling. In that case, the outer certificate binding extension should be critical.

comments.author: davidben
comments.body: Or possibly these are two separate extensions, one for the binding and a critical extension for the CA to say "I am wearing this hat".

comments.author: aarongable
comments.body:
I think the outer binding extension should be critical regardless: a relying party which is processing an embedded alternate certificate MUST understand and process the outer binding extension in order to prevent certificate mismatch issues.

If the webpki goes in the direction of the Alternate CA not actually performing validation, but instead just attesting that the Outer CA wants to issue this certificate, then I think that should be represented by a separate critical extension which indicates that validation was done by the Outer CA, not by the Alternate CA.

comments.author: davidben
comments.body:
Oh? I've no concerns making it critical, but I'm curious what certificate mismatch issue we're preventing.

From what I can see, if we don't ascribe extra semantics, making it critical just prevents someone from extracting the inner cert and then serving it directly. But I can't think of anything bad per se that would come of this. (Can't think of anything that it enables either.)

comments.author: aarongable
comments.body: Yep fair.

comments.author: davidben
comments.body: Closing this since it sounds like we'll solve this orthogonally, and #9 removed some of the explicit "both CAs validate stuff" text that made thing a bit awkward. Absent a reason to do it, I'm tempted to leave the outer binding extension non-critical; being able to extract the inner certificate standalone seems fine, and this is one less entry that your "do I recognize this critical extension" table needs to deal with.

issues.title: Issuer vs subject classification is a little odd for certificatePolicies
issues.author: davidben
issues.body:
@CBonnell pointed out an awkwardness. We currently say certificatePolicies is a subject extension, but then you get things like CA-specific EV OIDs and whatnot.

Possibly issuer vs subject is not the best name for the classification. What we really want is "are you allowed to swap this", with No constraining things and Yes adding some mismatch risk to the relying party. Here, since certificate policies is safe to swap out because you _already_ cannot interpret it without matching them up the chain, so a simple boolean result from your cert verification already wasn't sufficient.

issues.title: Does this require SCT?
issues.author: johngray-dev
issues.body:
The "issuing certificates" section seems to imply CT is not required, but then doesn't really describe how it works if CT is NOT used:

3. If the outer CA participates in Certificate Transparency (CT), it additionally signs a precertificate for its initial TBSCertificate, including the critical poison extension, as described in {{Section 3.1 of !RFC6962}}. The outer CA then requests Signed Certificate Timestamps (SCTs) from CT logs. This step MAY run in parallel with step 2.

4. The outer CA collects all AlternateIssuerInfos and SCTs and appends an `id-ce-embeddedSCT-CTv1` extension to its initial TBSCertificate.

If SCT's aren't used because it was in an enterprise PKI with many services (for example), they wouldn't have SCT's to embed.

The reason I point this out is because there is other text that seems to imply this isn't just for the web PKI:

"This document defines a mechanism to embed one or more alternate certificates within a single outer certificate. The outer certificate remains parseable to a legacy relying party that is unaware of this specification. Each alternate certificate certifies the same subject information, but with a different issuer. Rather than a general purpose mechanism, embedded alternate certificates are a temporary measure for PKI transitions, such as the post-quantum transition, in PKIs with significant legacy deployments."

However, that leads to an issue:  The AlternateIssuerInfos is embedded as a new type for TransItem structure, so that seems to imply that SCT's MUST be used, otherwise that information cannot be imbedded.   So then I read this as it required SCT's to reconstruct these certificates.    

If the above is correct, then it further constrains where this mechanism can be used, and we should make it clear that this is only applicable to PKI environments that use SCT's.

comments.author: davidben
comments.body:
Oh I didn't mean for it to require SCTs. Step 3 says "If the outer CA participates in Certificate Transparency (CT)", so you just skip the step if it's irrelevant. And then step 4 there was meant to be read as:

> 4\. The outer CA collects all AlternateIssuerInfos and SCTs (if any) and appends ...

It is necessary to encode the AlternateIssuerInfos as goofy SCTs, but if you otherwise don't use SCTs, you don't put anything else in there.

comments.author: johngray-dev
comments.body: Thanks David, that is much more clear now.

pulls.title: Simplify the text for issuing certificates
pulls.author: davidben
pulls.body:
Per discussion with @ounsworth today. How the two CA services communicate, whether they perform separate or combined validation, and even whether they are operated by the same entity or not, is all out of scope for this document.

Instead, focus on the mechanics of constructing the certificate. Rather than say things like "the alternate CA validates the TBSCertificate", say things like "the TBSCertificate MUST satisfy the policies of the alternate CA". This wording leaves enough room for either:

- Both CAs are operated by the same entity and the same domain validation applies to both, via some out-of-scope internal coordination.

- Via some out-of-scope mechanism, each CA independently performs domain validation.

I left the arrows in the (non-normative) diagram because I think they're useful for understanding the process, even if the exact nature of these arrows is situation-dependent. You can choose to interpret them as either actual messages being sent, or just dependency arrows.

(Also CC @aarongable because this is very related to something we were talking about the other day.)

comments.author: aarongable
comments.body: This reads much better to me.

comments.author: davidben
comments.body:
> I would prefer to frame it, instead of "each CA involved", as just "the CA", and the fact that "the CA" contains multiple issuers is internal detail of the CA that this document doesn't need to concern itself with.

So, the point of this PR is to not opine on whether the two CAs share an operator or not. Saying "the CA" means we're opining on it.

I think also what's happening is that what I call a "CA" you call an "issuer". What I call a "CA operator", you call a "CA".

I think "CA" in specifications refers to the particular issuer service, not the operator. For example, we say "intermediate certification authority". We don't say "intermediate issuer". Another example is that RFC 5280 includes clauses like:

> There is one exception; where a CA distributes its public key in the form of a "self-signed" certificate, the authority key identifier MAY be omitted.

If the "CA" were the overarching entity that ran multiple issuing services, you cannot talk about "its public key" because there are multiple ones. It only make senses if the "CA" is the single issuer.

Just noodling here: the presentation flow is basically:

* Construct Outer TBSCert
* Construct Inner TBSCert
* Sign Inner TBSCert
* Stuff Inner TBSCert into Outer TBSCert
* Sign Outer TBSCert

It would be a simpler flow if it was:

* Construct & Sign Inner TBSCert
* Construct & Sign Outer TBSCert (including Inner as an extn)
Of course, you need the more complicated flow for the inner-to-outer binding. ... maybe?
Bullet numbering is out of order. Maybe this renders fine in HTML, but should probably be fixed.

reviews.author: ounsworth
reviews.body:
I'm fine to merge this for -00, but I suggest that we could simplify this even further. For example:

> After subject information is validated according to the policies of each CA involved, the certificates are issued in the following process:

I would prefer to frame it, instead of "each CA involved", as just "the CA", and the fact that "the CA" contains multiple issuers is internal detail of the CA that this document doesn't need to concern itself with.

comments.body: The more complicated flow is needed for the binding, yes. But also this flow just fits into what the CAs are *already* doing for SCTs, so I don't think this is particularly costly.
Seems correct to me. The 4 above is from an indented child list, not the outer list.

More importantly, this whole construction is based on the idea that the entity requesting the cert (the Subscriber) has no idea that this is going on in the background. Therefore, by definition, the Subscriber must be communicating with the Outer CA. It's not possible for the Inner CA to construct the inner cert first, because they don't know what the contents of that cert should be until the Outer CA communicates with them.

pulls.title: I re-wrote the intro
pulls.author: ounsworth
pulls.body:
* I did big snip snip on the Intro :) Focused on a concise description of the problem statement.
* Added a section "Detailed Design Requirements" where we can lock-in precisely what we are trying to design here.
* I added a cheeky title "Smuggled Nested Additional-Issuer Layer (SNAIL) Certificates"
* I systematically renamed "alternate issuer" to "additional issuer" to reflect that these are not supposed to be a totally isolated certs.
* I started renaming "issuer" to "certification path" where it makes sense; because the core idea is that you have one subject name / public key that gets captured in two (or more) different (but coupled) sets of TA -> ICA -> EE Cert. I think "certification path" is a better mental picture for that than "issuer".


---

BTW; I am still not convinced that the inner-to-outer binding is necessary, but we can sort that out later. Like, I'm not convinced that there's a serious security issue associated with split-views in the RP beyond what can be handled by saying "BAD CA!" if they issue certs that lead to weird behaviours.

I suggest that we spend some cycles just on the Detailed Design Requirements before getting too into the exact shape of the solution.

comments.author: davidben
comments.body:
Haven't looked at the PR yet, just some quick thoughts from the preamble:

> I added a cheeky title "Smuggled Nested Additional-Issuer Layer (SNAIL) Certificates"

Hehehe. Chameleons, fowl, and now snails. Just how many animals do we have in this zoo? 🤣 

More seriously, I think it's worth avoiding "smuggled" just to avoid any funny connotations. Which, you know, is coming from someone who called it a "turducken", but I did try to keep "turducken" out of the _official_ name. 🙃

> I systematically renamed "alternate issuer" to "additional issuer" to reflect that these are not supposed to be a totally isolated certs.

Ah interesting. I went for "alternate" at first to capture this is an alternate choice from the relying party's perspective. That is, the relying party is expected to validate one _or_ the other. "Additional" seems to suggest the relying party checks this certificate _in addition to_ the outer one. But the relying party in this model probably doesn't even trust the outer CA anymore because the key's been compromised by a CRQC.

Thoughts?

> BTW; I am still not convinced that the inner-to-outer binding is necessary, but we can sort that out later. Like, I'm not convinced that there's a serious security issue associated with split-views in the RP beyond what can be handled by saying "BAD CA!" if they issue certs that lead to weird behaviours.

The inner-to-outer binding is what lets us say "BAD CA!" in the first place. Otherwise the attack doesn't involve the CA doing anything wrong in the first place. Concretely:

1. Attacker owns `attacker.example` and gets alternate CA to sign `attacker.example` with attacker's private key. This is a perfectly valid certificate. The attacker legitimately owns both.

2. Attacker constructs the following outer certificate

   * SPKI is the attacker's SPKI.
   * SAN is `example.com`.
   * AlternateIssuerInfo specifies to remove the `example.com` SAN and replace it with `attacker.example`
   * Issuer and signature are arbitrary. Doesn't matter because it's not someone the RP trusts anyway.

If the relying party does not enforce anything about extensions (because that has the fail-closed problem we were talking about), this will reconstruct the attacker's legitimate certificate as the alternate certificate and check out. But a split-view relying party will then look at outer certificate and go "aha the attacker's SPKI is authoritative for `example.com`" and badness ensues.

Zero CAs did anything bad to enable this. The attacker's certificate is totally legitimate. The CA that the RP trusted never signed over the fact that it was part of this transformation. The point of the outer binding is ensure that they do. _Then_ this scenario is not possible without CA involvement.

But, like you say, we can also sort it out later.

comments.author: ounsworth
comments.body:
"Alternate" vs "Additional":

> That is, the relying party is expected to validate one or the other. "Additional" seems to suggest the relying party checks this certificate in addition to the outer one. 

This is exactly the core point that I think we need to figure out clarity on -- after that, I suspect the rest will click into place -- is it an AND mode or an OR mode? Or is it neither of those things in a way that we can figure out how to describe concisely?

From a legacy client's perspective, it only sees one thing, so calling that on OR mode is a bit confusing -- it only sees one thing!

And from the upgraded client's perspective, there are two things, but the inner-to-outer binding to solve split-views means that it's not an OR mode there either; but it's also not an AND mode; it's something in between, and my usual mental model for thinking about these things breaks.

Like, I'm not even sure that I can explain this to myself in a clear and concise way, let alone get on a stage and explain it to a room full of people, and this is the core stumbling block.

comments.author: ounsworth
comments.body:
> The inner-to-outer binding is what lets us say "BAD CA!" in the first place.

> 2. Attacker constructs the following outer certificate

I am starting to suspect that there are some pre-assumptions about the attack scenario / threat model that you have in your head that do not match mine.

Presumably, Outer is still CT-logged, and therefore leaves an artifact to researchers to find and say "BAD CA!".

Presumably, Outer CA is not so compromised that the attacker effectively has its private key and can sign arbitrary certs (and ditto for the signing key of the CT log). Surely if that's in-scope for the security model, and you're assuming that parts of your upgraded client still have that thing in their trust store, then surely we have bigger problems than split views? 

I'm softof inclined to say that a partially-upgraded client that has some layers where the legacy TAs are removed and some where they are still trusted is just a vulnerable client. I understand that this will be an intermediate migration state than many platforms will go through, so I think this should work for well-behaved turducken certs where everything lines up like it's supposed to, but I'm not convinced that we should be be overly-complicating the spec to try and protect against maliciously-constructed certs that exploit this; because I think it's not fundamentally different from any other non-upgraded vulnerable client.

What we could do is include some negative test vectors where Inner and Outer have different SANs, different EKUs, etc, and say _"If your client chokes on this, then means that you haven't found all the places that you need to upgrade; keep going"_.

comments.author: davidben
comments.body:
It's an OR mode. That seems pretty clear to me? The client accepts the certificate if it accepts the outer certificate OR the alternate certificate.

Yes, legacy clients will always pick the first half of the OR because they are incapable of doing anything else. Newer clients will... in principle evaluate both, but we intend for them to take the alternate certificate in the long run, since their goal is to stop depending on classical CAs.

The inner-to-outer binding isn't about OR vs AND. Or rather, it is needed _because_ it's an OR mode. Because _some_ clients will _only_ verify the inner signature, the outer certificate parts are suddenly malleable.

Does it matter that it's malleable? Well, if you're doing an OR mode, the client needs to consistently apply all its access checks on the branch of the OR that it took. However, due to non-browser scenarios where the client has different parts updated at different times, we risk a security vulnerability if the client gets a bit confused. The inner-to-outer binding is to keep the outer certificate non-malleable even if the client:

* Looked at the inner certificate
* Has some components that got a bit confused

I think this is important because IMO clients that are not browsers should have a path to PQ-security too.

> Presumably, Outer CA is not so compromised that the attacker effectively has its private key and can sign arbitrary certs (and ditto for the signing key of the CT log). Surely if that's in-scope for the security model, and you're assuming that parts of your upgraded client still have that thing in their trust store, then surely we have bigger problems than split views?

Ah yes, that is the mismatch. I am assuming the Outer CA is indeed so compromised. The Outer CA is a classical CA and every CRQC is presumed to have its private key. CT logging doesn't save us because the CT signatures are themselves classical signatures, and so the attacker is presumed to have the CT signing keys too.

The system needs to be secure even if that happens. I.e. the PQ client is totally ignoring the outer certificate's signatures (because it gets no value from them anyway) and needs to get all the assurance it needs from the alternate certificate's signatures.

comments.author: ounsworth
comments.body: (note, I edited my previous text while you were posting yours. Might want to re-read it)

comments.author: ounsworth
comments.body:
> It's an OR mode. That seems pretty clear to me? The client accepts the certificate if it accepts the outer certificate OR the alternate certificate.

Maybe we don't agree on the definition of "OR mode" lol.

I think the logic we're defining is:

* The legacy client accepts the outer certificate. It never had a choice.
* The upgraded client accepts the alternate certificate, but only after checking the outer cert for consistency via the inner-to-outer.

Neither of those things sound like a nice clean "OR" to me. ...
To my understanding, the inner-to-outer binding is what complicates it from not being a clean OR.

comments.author: davidben
comments.body:
> The upgraded client accepts the alternate certificate, but only after checking the outer cert for consistency via the inner-to-outer.

Hmm. So the upgraded client isn't *checking* anything for the binding. That's why I like the binding more than the extension classification. (Extension classification is actually a check.)

All the upgraded client is doing is appending an extension as part of the process to compute the alternate certificate in the first place. That is, the outer binding doesn't show up in `issuerExtensions` at all. It's just that one of the steps in applying the delta is to add this extra extension based on some values you saved along the way.

Once you've done that, you have the alternate certificate, which happens to, by how you reconstructed it, always have an outer binding extension. Then you pass that to your unmodified path validator, which will check the signature over it because it happens to be inside the TBSCertificate.

comments.author: ounsworth
comments.body:
> Ah yes, that is the mismatch. I am assuming the Outer CA is indeed so compromised. The Outer CA is a classical CA and every CRQC is presumed to have its private key.

This is a productive discussion! Mental Models Align!

Ok. Start with basics. I think we both agree that under this security model, we'll keep serving content to your 2010 Smart TV with 2010 roots, but nobody is pretending that there's any security there. Agree?

I think we both agree that a fully upgraded RP won't have this split-view problem because either every layer understands and is using the inner cert, or some layer doesn't understand the nested cert and doesn't have the outer TA and so hard-fails (nothing we can do about that).

The split-view problem comes in with a partially-upgraded client that is still only partially upgraded after Q-Day. My vote (currently, I reserve the right to change my mind) is that that's a "Fix Your Stack" problem, that's a "You're not a 2010 TV, why do you even still have these TAs?" problem, and not something that we should be including within the security model of the draft.

comments.body:
**I SEE**

So, actually, "split-view" is the wrong name for the vulnerability, it's more: clients that validate the cert using a turducken-aware parser, then raw-ASN.1 parse the cert and grab the outer SANs, or whatever.. To be fair, the application might not be completely reparsing the certificate. Maybe it's got `X509` object from OpenSSL and is just inspecting it a bit. Not totally far-fetched if the extension doesn't interact with path validation, so the path builder component doesn't support it.

Here's a maybe more plausible strawman: an application uses the LogoType extension from [RFC 9399](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9399/) (hahaha why...). `id-pe-logotype` doesn't interact with path building in any way, so the path verifier doesn't implement it at all. Rather, the application verifies with OpenSSL, and then extracts the logotype extension. If it looks at the wrong one, it won't get the logo that the CA actually signed over.

This is also an example where the binding is more robust than extension checking. In the extension-checking model, we expect OpenSSL to say "no, `id-pe-logotype` is a subject extension, so it may not be changed". But OpenSSL doesn't support this extension (it has no need to). If it doesn't know the extension, it can't possibly enforce it, unless it rejects all unknown extensions, but then we have the extensibility problem.

In the binding version, it's OK if OpenSSL doesn't enforce anything because, if `id-pe-logotype` was perturbed, the outer value will end up in the binding extension. That means one of two things will happen:
* The signature doesn't check out because the alternate CA never signed over that
* The signature checks out because the alternate CA _did_ sign over that. But if it did, _then_ we get to say "BAD CA!"

Anyway, this is possibly getting in the weeds a bit. :-) Popping up the stack... did that help us answer the "alternate" or "additional" question? :-)

pulls.author: davidben

This rewrites the introduction to be shorter and follow the flow in Mike Ounsworth's PR #11.

My old introduction tried to motivate things super generally, and then interleaved a detailed story of the post-quantum transition. Aha! Good call. I'm glad you pointed this out. That is a subtle distinction that I'd inadvertently been glossing over all this time.

I'll tug on this phrasing slightly, which will maybe help draw a finer line here:

> It is proving that it possess a traditional key and is allowed to use it. Nothing more, nothing less.

It's proving something slightly more. It's proving that the service owner both possesses a traditional key *and has authorized the PQ CA to sign it*. By doing that, the service owner is saying "I would like modern clients to trust this traditional key for my service".

You're right that the service owner _could_ have a PQ key and still say that. Though that's a dumb thing to do because it enables downgrade. We _expect_ that service owners will stop doing that once they're PQ-capable.

While we still expect a PQ-capable service to have both a traditional key and a PQ key, we _expect_ them to _only_ authorize the PQ CA to sign over PQ keys. The traditional key is only authorized to the traditional CAs. That way the service does not make up-to-date clients vulnerable to its traditional key.

And so specifically this is a quantum-resistant proof that the service is in the first category and not the second. Put another way, our goal is to give the service owners the tools to make themselves PQ-secure. As long as the PQ CA faithfully signs only what was authorized, those tools exist.

Let's try this. Probably could do with wordsmithing, but I think this captures the goal and also your point:

```suggestion
1. Legacy services serve certificates with post-quantum issuers, even if the end entity keys are still traditional. This is known as a *post-quantum opt-out certificate*. It provides a quantum-resistant proof to the relying party that the service has authorized a traditional end entity key for upgraded relying parties. (It is expected that only services that are not yet post-quantum-capable will authorize such certificates. A securely-configured post-quantum-capable service would authorize only its post-quantum key with post-quantum issuers, leaving its traditional key for traditional issuers and legacy relying parties.)
```

How about we just spell out the trivializing factor then, so people don't have to read between the lines?

```suggestion
An outer certificate with many AlternateIssuerInfo structures can require more processing time in the relying party. This is similar to path building itself {{?RFC4158}}, X.509 policy validation {{?RFC9618}}, certification path length, and other factors that contribute to X.509 scaling. Relying parties SHOULD limit the number of alternate certificates in a single outer certificate they will process. For example, if the relying party has a path building iteration limit, considering an alternate certificate can contribute to that limit. An attacker can inject arbitrarily many AlternateIssuerInfo structures into an unverified outer certificate, so this avoids a denial of service vector.
```
